mcqs.question: Which statement correctly defines a covalent bond and distinguishes it from an ionic bond?

options.A: In a covalent bond, atoms share electron pairs; in an ionic bond, electrons are transferred from one atom to another.
options.B: In a covalent bond, electrons are transferred; in an ionic bond, atoms share electron pairs.
options.C: Both covalent and ionic bonds involve sharing of electrons equally.
options.D: Covalent bonds occur only between metals, while ionic bonds occur only between non‑metals.

mcqs.answer: In a covalent bond, atoms share electron pairs; in an ionic bond, electrons are transferred from one atom to another.
mcqs.explanation: A covalent bond is formed when two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons, achieving stability without full electron transfer. In contrast, an ionic bond results from the complete transfer of electrons from a metal to a non‑metal, creating oppositely charged ions that attract each other. Options B, C, and D describe incorrect definitions or restrictions.

mcqs.question: Which electron‑dot structure correctly represents a methane (CH₄) molecule?

options.A: C surrounded by four single lines each ending in H; no dots on H.
options.B: C with two lone pairs and two single lines to H.
options.C: C with three single lines to H and one double bond to H.
options.D: C with a triple bond to H and one single bond to H.

mcqs.answer: C surrounded by four single lines each ending in H; no dots on H.
mcqs.explanation: Methane consists of a central carbon atom sharing one electron pair with each of four hydrogen atoms, giving four C–H single bonds. No lone pairs remain on carbon or hydrogen. Options B, C, and D depict incorrect numbers of bonds or lone pairs.

mcqs.learning_point: Relate bonding to diversity of carbon compounds
mcqs.question: How does carbon’s tetravalency contribute to the large variety of its compounds?

options.A: It allows carbon to form up to four covalent bonds, enabling the construction of chains, branches, and rings.
options.B: It restricts carbon to combine only with hydrogen, limiting diversity.
options.C: It forces carbon to form only double bonds, reducing possible structures.
options.D: It makes carbon only able to bond with oxygen atoms.

mcqs.answer: It allows carbon to form up to four covalent bonds, enabling the construction of chains, branches, and rings.
mcqs.explanation: Because carbon can form four covalent bonds, it can link to other carbon atoms and various other elements in many ways—linear, branched, cyclic, and with multiple bond types—producing the vast array of organic molecules. Options B, C, and D incorrectly limit carbon’s bonding capability.

mcqs.question: A carbon atom in a molecule is already bonded to three other atoms. According to the concept of tetravalency, what can this carbon atom do next?

options.A: Form a fourth covalent bond with another atom.
options.C: Break one of the existing bonds to stay tetravalent.
options.D: Remain with only three bonds because carbon can have a maximum of three bonds.

mcqs.answer: Form a fourth covalent bond with another atom.
mcqs.explanation: Tetravalency means carbon can have exactly four covalent bonds. If it already has three, it can form one more to satisfy the rule. Forming a fifth bond or breaking a bond to stay at three violates tetravalency, and carbon never remains with only three bonds when a fourth partner is available.

mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about catenation is incorrect?

options.A: Catenation is the ability of carbon atoms to bond with each other forming long chains and rings.
options.B: Catenation allows carbon to form only linear chains, not branched structures.
options.C: Catenation is possible because carbon can form strong C–C covalent bonds.
options.D: Catenation contributes to the vast number of organic compounds.

mcqs.answer: Catenation allows carbon to form only linear chains, not branched structures.
mcqs.explanation: Catenation refers to carbon’s ability to bond to other carbon atoms, producing both linear and branched chains as well as rings. Option B incorrectly limits catenation to only linear structures, while the other options correctly describe the concept.

mcqs.question: Why does carbon readily form covalent bonds with other carbon atoms to create stable chains?

options.A: Because the C–C single bond has a high bond dissociation energy, making the bond strong and stable.
options.B: Because carbon atoms have a full outer shell and do not need to share electrons.
options.C: Because carbon atoms are metallic and conduct electricity.
options.D: Because C–C bonds are ionic in nature.

mcqs.answer: Because the C–C single bond has a high bond dissociation energy, making the bond strong and stable.
mcqs.explanation: The C–C single bond is strong (≈ 348 kJ mol⁻¹), so chains of carbon atoms are energetically favorable and stable. Options B, C, and D mischaracterize carbon’s electronic configuration and the nature of C–C bonds.

mcqs.question: Which pair of electron‑dot structures correctly shows the difference between carbon dioxide (CO₂) and carbon tetrachloride (CCl₄)?

options.A: CO₂: C double bonded to O on both sides, each O with two lone pairs; CCl₄: C single bonded to four Cl atoms, each Cl with three lone pairs.
options.B: CO₂: C single bonded to two O atoms, each O with one lone pair; CCl₄: C double bonded to two Cl atoms and single bonded to two Cl atoms.
options.C: CO₂: C triple bonded to one O and single bonded to another O; CCl₄: C single bonded to four H atoms.
options.D: CO₂: C with four lone pairs, no bonds; CCl₄: C with no bonds, surrounded by Cl atoms.

mcqs.answer: CO₂: C double bonded to O on both sides, each O with two lone pairs; CCl₄: C single bonded to four Cl atoms, each Cl with three lone pairs.
mcqs.explanation: In CO₂, carbon forms two double bonds (C=O) and each oxygen has two lone pairs. In CCl₄, carbon forms four single bonds (C–Cl) and each chlorine has three lone pairs. The other options misrepresent bond types or atoms involved.

mcqs.learning_point: Relate bonding to diversity of carbon compounds
mcqs.question: Which statement best explains why carbon’s ability to catenate leads to the greatest diversity of organic compounds among the elements?

options.A: Carbon can form strong C–C single, double, and triple bonds, allowing the formation of straight chains, branched chains, and rings of varying lengths.
options.B: Carbon can only form single bonds with other carbon atoms, limiting the variety of structures.
options.C: Carbon’s catenation is weak, so it rarely forms long chains.
options.D: Only hydrogen can catenate, not carbon.

mcqs.answer: Carbon can form strong C–C single, double, and triple bonds, allowing the formation of straight chains, branched chains, and rings of varying lengths.
mcqs.explanation: Carbon’s ability to make single, double, and triple C–C bonds, all of which are strong, enables an enormous number of possible skeletons—linear, branched, cyclic, and of varying lengths—accounting for the vast diversity of organic molecules. Options B, C, and D are factually incorrect.
